title: Explain the Circuit Breaker pattern states (Closed/Open/Half-Open), how you tune thresholds/timeouts/reset-time, whether the breaker can be a single point of failure, how to prevent cascading failures across chained breakers, pitfalls in async/Kafka systems, the fallback-depends-on-failing-service trap, adaptive breakers, and when a breaker is harmful.
shortTitle: Circuit Breaker pattern: Closed, Open, Half-Open states, tuning, pitfalls, and when it is harmful
topicTitle: Behavioral: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template
keyPoints: Closed means calls flow normally and failures are counted; Open means fail fast without calling the dependency; Half-Open means cautiously test if the dependency recovered.
The failure-rate threshold, per-call timeout, and wait duration in open state are the three key tuning parameters.
Combine the breaker with timeouts and bulkheads to prevent cascading failures across chained services.
The fallback must be genuinely independent of the failing service; a cache populated by the failing service is useless.
In async/Kafka systems, tripping a breaker means pausing consumption or routing to a dead-letter queue, not throwing to a caller.
A breaker is harmful when it guards something cheap and reliable, or when it hides a real bug that should be fixed.

s1_definition.oneliner: Closed means try normally, Open means fail fast and do not call, Half-Open means cautiously test if the dependency has recovered.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Circuit Breaker** – a stability pattern that wraps a call to a fragile dependency and monitors it for failures.
- **Closed state** – calls flow normally; the breaker counts failures in a sliding window.
- **Open state** – failures exceeded the threshold; all calls are immediately rejected or routed to a fallback.
- **Half-Open state** – after a reset timeout, a few trial calls are allowed to test if the dependency recovered.
- **Resilience4j** – the most popular Java circuit-breaker library, configuring thresholds, windows, and wait durations.
- **Purpose** – protects both the caller and the struggling dependency from cascading failure.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the electrical circuit breaker in Rajesh's house. Normally electricity flows freely: that is Closed. If there is a dangerous surge, the breaker trips and cuts the power: that is Open. After some time Rajesh flips it back carefully to test if things are safe: that is Half-Open. In banking, the "electricity" is a call to the CIBIL credit-score service. If CIBIL is down and every loan request keeps waiting thirty seconds and failing, the whole loan service grinds to a halt. The circuit breaker trips so loan requests fail fast with a fallback.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Circuit Breaker pattern is a stability pattern that wraps a call to a fragile dependency and watches for failures. It has three states. In Closed, calls flow normally and the breaker counts failures. When failures cross a threshold, it trips to Open, where it fails fast without calling the dependency. After a reset timeout it moves to Half-Open, letting a few trial calls through to test recovery.

In the loan approval service at National Bank of India, the CIBIL credit-score API was the fragile dependency. During an outage every call hung for thirty seconds, threatening to take down the whole loan service. Pankaj put a circuit breaker around the call so that once CIBIL started failing, requests failed fast and fell back to a conservative internal rule, stopping one sick dependency from cascading into a full outage.

On tuning, the failure-rate threshold, per-call timeout, and wait duration in open state are the three key parameters. Combining the breaker with bulkheads isolates the thread pool so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads. The fallback must be genuinely independent of the failing service, because a cache populated by CIBIL is useless when CIBIL is down.

The two traps to call out are async systems and harmful breakers. In Kafka-based flows, a breaker does not throw to a caller; instead you pause consumption or route to a dead-letter topic. And a breaker is harmful when it guards something cheap and reliable, when the threshold is so sensitive it trips on normal blips, or when it hides a real bug that should be fixed. Use a battle-tested library like Resilience4j and keep breaker state per instance so the breaker itself never becomes a single point of failure.

Remember one sentence: the Circuit Breaker monitors a fragile dependency and fails fast when failures exceed a threshold, protecting the caller and the dependency from cascading failure.
